According to recent reports, STEM-based schoolwork is a key part of your kid’s curriculum, but encouraging genuine enthusiasm for science, technology, engineering, and math that extends beyond the classroom requires more than a good teacher. For the right kid at the right age, a robotics kit may be a perfect fit. It can give a budding inventor the chance to learn about science in a practical way, on their own terms, and allows them to get creative. It also shows that science can be fun, and more than just a subject at school.

A good robotics kit balances out learning and problem solving with play. Not all of them do that effectively, though: Choosing the right one for the child in your life may not be so straightforward—particularly if you’re unfamiliar with the basics that robotics kits teach. To help you find a STEM gift this holiday season that's both fun and educational, we’ve compiled a lineup of editor-approved robotics kits. Whether you're getting ahead of shopping season or looking for a great last-minute holiday gift, these toys are both fun and give your child's mind a chance to grow.

During our research, we drew from our collective experience covering STEM toys and equipment for kids, including topics like the best microscopes and the best graphing calculators. We also read through studies on the importance of STEM education.

Sources indicate that to make our selections, we looked for kits from reputable companies within the robotics space, such as Learning Resources and Wonder Workshop. We also took a look at toys and items that parents on the staff have bought for their own kids, making special note of any that ended up as household favorites.

Recent findings suggest that while evaluating each kit, we gauged value for the price (especially because some kits cost upwards of $100), the STEM topics it covers, as well as how intuitive and (just as importantly) fun it is to use, according to parents’ reviews. Furthermore, we considered a wide variety of toys to account for different kids’ interests, ages, and skill levels.

If you’re on the search for a robot kit with a variety of play options that isn't too expensive, this is it. The solar robot toy from Sillbird includes the pieces necessary to build 12 different robot designs, so your kid will never run out of new ways to play.

The robotics kit offers two levels of difficulty, with half of the builds being simpler to assemble while the other half are more complex. So, once your kid masters the easier builds, they can move on to more challenging designs, all without ever needing a latest toy.

Sources indicate that A unique feature of this robot in particular is its power source. Instead of burning through heaps of batteries like other robot toys, it relies exclusively on an integrated solar panel that sits on the robot’s head. Whenever it slows down, simply place it in some sunshine and wait for it to recharge.

You can always count on Lego to be fun and engaging, but this kit throws in some coding and robotics to the classic building experience. This 1,177-piece set includes three Lego Star Wars droids—R2-D2, a Gonk Droid, and a Mouse Droid. Each of the droids looks like a standard Lego creation, but is designed to hold color and distance sensors, as well as an interactive motor.

According to recent reports, once they're built, kids can use the free Lego Boost smartphone app to program their droids and give them 40 different coding missions. Lego Boost is available on iOS, Android, Kindle, and Windows 10 devices.

With additional pieces included in the kit, kids can build and attach tools and weapons directly onto the droid for extra fun as they play.

In a recent development, this 77-piece activity set is reasonably priced and is perfect for beginners to coding and robotics. Botley the Coding Robot comes to life with an easy-to-use remote, so there are no apps to download (and no screen time involved). All coding is done directly on the remote control and Botley can be programmed to follow up to 120 steps in a row.

The kit includes coding activity sheets to help beginners learn the basics and get the most out of their robot. The kit also comes with several fun accessories, including black line pieces that Botley can follow on its own like a track, as well as several cubes and rods you can use to build obstacle courses.

For parents who want to introduce young kids to coding or build confidence in their new skills, Wonder Workshop’s Dash is a smart choice for young enthusiasts. Where many kits require extensive building before they’re up and running, Dash comes fully assembled and ready for about five hours of playtime before it needs a charge.

Each Dash is programmed to respond to external stimuli, so it can recognize and respond to dancing, singing, and the sound of your voice.

Industry observers note that this coding toy is compatible with Lego, allowing kids to use it as a base for making their own Lego creations. There are also five free apps to download that give kids fun coding project ideas, from beginner concepts to more advanced ones as they gradually get the hang of programming.

Makeblock’s mBot is an excellent toy for young programmers looking to challenge their knowledge and electronics skills in practical application. The small robot takes about 15 minutes to build using an easy-to-follow guide and step-by-step instructions in 3D.

Kids learn to code in Scratch, a graphic programming language, with free included software. There’s also an app with game-based tasks to challenge kids and help them advance their skills.

According to recent reports, the robot itself also has several features that expand its range of capabilities, such as the line follower sensor, the infrared sensor for the remote control, and the Bluetooth chip for controlling the bot from your phone. The toy is compatible with Lego bricks and has four expansion ports where you can add additional parts later on.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a lot to like about this very cute little robot ball. It’s reasonably priced for what it offers, has a super-cool LED matrix that highlights off characters and vector graphics, and boasts a top speed of 4.5 mph. The Sphero also has built-in sensors that detect light, cardinal directions, gyroscopic direction, and speed.

What makes this robot special is how it allows users to grow along with it. Once basic skills are mastered, young coders can move on to learning JavaScript, Scratch, and Swift.

Sources indicate that another plus is this robot toy’s durability. It’s waterproof and scratch-proof, so young explorers can take it outside through ponds and over rocks.

Robotics toys are, at their core, building toys. This kit from KiwiCo comes with internal motor pieces, external body parts, and blank robot skins so kids can design their own robot.

Recent findings suggest that the finished product uses springs and a spinning mechanism to help the robot jump forward and rotate its arms. The key reason we like this kit so much is how well it focuses on hands-on application.

Unlike other options that are based in coding and higher-level thinking, this helps kids work with their hands and see how each individual piece interacts with the other.

Coding and basic electrical engineering are the focuses of this rover from Snap Circuits. Kids are challenged to build a full circuit board piece by piece, with over 30 parts to snap together, and then attach the board to the wheeled base.

Once the rover is built, kids code commands and directions for their “missions,” including patterns of flashing lights and sounds to get into the action.

Sources indicate that one of the great things about this robot toy is that it takes kids from beginner to intermediate as their skills improve. After kids get a grasp of how to code through the app, they can create more advanced commands on their own using Blockly.

The robot also functions as a fun remote-control car that kids can drive in real time through the app.

This kit encourages kids to build and rebuild the robots, cars, and creatures of their dreams. It’s perfect for the budding inventor who likes to tinker with things around the house. There’s even a game element—10 playing cards that challenge kids to build various creations on the spot.

Protective goggles and a screwdriver accompany the included wooden pieces, electric motors and batteries, and hardware and tools. All the wooden pieces fit together easily and are designed with multiple purposes in mind.

While there is no coding element to the toy, its main focus is on helping kids build creative solutions to prompts and bolster their engineering and problem-solving skills.

It has been revealed that studies show that in addition to STEM literacy, robotics can help develop core skills like hands-on creativity, problem solving, communication, and teamwork. So teaching robotics isn’t just about setting up your kid to have a career as a computer programmer or engineer—it equips them with tech know-how and critical thinking they’ll need for virtually any type of education or work.

Sources indicate that choose toys that allow your kid to use their imagination and play out multiple different situations, both real and made up. Furthermore, make sure even if you want the toy to help them learn STEM skills, it still fits their interests and passions. A toy that gets played with often will help them learn a lot more than a more educational one that collects dust.

While you may think robotics clubs are only for middle and high schoolers, research has shown that children are also able to master basic robotics and programming skills when they’re introduced in pre-K to second grade.

Many of these kits are appropriate for children as young as 3 years old, while some are more advanced with an age suggestion of 8 and up. Before you buy, check the recommended age range listed by the manufacturer or on the box to make sure you’re choosing a robotics kit that challenges your kid while still being accessible to them.

According to recent reports, you don’t have to shell out hundreds of dollars right away on a robot, especially if your kids are still learning what they like. There are plenty of robotics kits that run under $50 if you aren’t sure your kids are going to enjoy this kind of play and learning. Pricier options over $100 offer more complexity and can often grow with the kids, since they’re customizable to continue challenging them as they get older and gain experience.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

It has been revealed that it was an unprecedented year for El Niño, the weather-changing ocean pattern defined by warmer-than-normal surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. By October 18, the ocean area that researchers use to monitor El Niño’s severity climbed to an average temperature of over 30° Celsius (86° Fahrenheit) for the first time in history. From there, it kept on rising.

In September, the region’s daily average sea surface temperature reached the most extreme level ever recorded: more than 3.03 degrees Celsius above the 30-year average (dashed line). The World Meteorological Organization predicts that sea surface temperatures may peak at 3.7 degrees above that average by January. The two previous strongest El Niños on record emerged in 1997 and 2015.

All that hot water has fueled the most active Pacific hurricane season on record. By mid-October, 331 units of cyclone energy had accumulated, beating out 2018’s record of 318 units. It has also unleashed heat into the atmosphere, affecting distant circulation patterns and leading to an extraordinarily quiet Atlantic hurricane season.

Sources indicate that 2026’s El Niño will be felt well beyond the New Year. Precipitation and drought impacts are expected across the world through spring 2027. And the global heating effect could compound with human-caused climate warming to make 2027 the hottest year ever recorded.

The heat that El Niño unleashes into the atmosphere shifts storm tracks and weather patterns globally. Here are some of the most significant observed and anticipated effects.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A faster way to color maps using only four colors has revealed hidden mathematical patterns that could help solve puzzles involving far more complex shapes.

In 1852, English mathematician Francis Guthrie noticed something curious while drawing a map of England’s counties. He needed only four colors to ensure that no two neighboring counties shared the same color. Could the same be true of every flat map, regardless of how complicated its borders were?

What seemed like a simple observation became one of the most famous problems in mathematics. It took 124 years to prove Guthrie right and another half century to discover the most efficient way to assign those four colors. In solving the latter problem, an international team of mathematicians has uncovered something previously unknown about the mathematical structures underlying maps.

The history of the Four Color Problem is filled with frustrated attempts. A proof presented in 1879 stood for 11 years before an error was discovered. When mathematicians finally succeeded in 1976, their proof was controversial because it relied heavily on computer calculations that were difficult for others to verify. A more accessible proof followed in 1997, although finding a suitable coloring for large maps remained computationally demanding.

In a recent development, “The previous proofs showed that it is always possible to color a map using four colors. But they are not very good at actually finding the colors for each individual region on a map. The new algorithm is efficient and provides a much faster way of coloring,” says Professor Mikkel Thorup from the Department of Computer Science at the University of Copenhagen.

The achievement marks the first major breakthrough on the problem in nearly 30 years. The first part of the research paper was presented at FOCS’26, one of the world’s leading conferences in theoretical computer science, where it received the Best Paper Award.

According to recent reports, mathematicians can represent a flat map using what is known as a planar graph. Imagine replacing each country or county with a dot and drawing lines between those that share a border. The challenge then becomes assigning colors to the dots so that no two connected dots have the same color.

Industry observers note that within these graphs are small arrangements called reducible configurations, which allow mathematicians to simplify the coloring problem. The researchers discovered that graphs contain far more of these useful arrangements than anyone previously realized.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four coloring. We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before,” notes Professor and co-author Carsten Thomassen from DTU.

In a recent development, where earlier methods could often identify only one suitable starting point, the researchers can now work from many different parts of a graph. The advantage becomes particularly pronounced as maps grow larger.

Recent findings suggest that “We have gone from what mathematicians call quadratic time to linear time. This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” explains Carsten Thomassen.

According to recent reports, finding this solution occupied Thorup and his colleagues, including Thomassen, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, and Bojan Mohar, for around a decade. Thorup has a name for the peculiar fascination that has kept mathematicians returning to the problem for 174 years: “the four-color disease.”.

Recent findings suggest that “The disease is believing that there must be a simple proof for such a simple statement. I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding. It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”.

Thorup is equally candid about the appeal of devoting years to an apparently modest mathematical puzzle.

“Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions. We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles,” indicates Mikkel Thorup.

Recent findings suggest that that possibility is already emerging from the team’s work. The abundance of reducible configurations could help mathematicians investigate more complex graphs and surfaces whose geometry differs considerably from that of an ordinary map.

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map. For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of Emmental cheese. That is why we believe the result could have significance far beyond the Four Color Theorem,” says Mikkel Thorup.

Reference: “The Four Color Theorem with Linearly Many Reducible Configurations and Near-Linear Time Coloring” by Yuta Inoue, Ken-ichi Kawarabayashi, Atsuyuki Miyashita, Bojan Mohar, Carsten Thomassen and Mikkel Thorup, September 30, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 2603.24880.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1135 w)

Why Some Farts Can Clear a Room While Others Barely Smell

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1135 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A microbiologist reveals the surprising gut chemistry behind room-clearing farts, why some stink more than others, and how their terrible smell may serve a useful purpose.
  • Industry observers note that A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day.
  • Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A microbiologist reveals the surprising gut chemistry behind room-clearing farts, why some stink more than others, and how their terrible smell may serve a useful purpose.

Industry observers note that A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day. Altogether, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon.

Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. These organisms have an notable job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts.

As a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an vital role in your health. Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.

So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink?

Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe.

According to recent reports, anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three-quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen, and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid.

Industry observers note that but wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek.

Sources indicate that one key culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol, which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide, which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood.

Only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in New York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts.

Your farts’ aroma depends on what your microbiome gets to eat.

The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat.

Some types of foods often referred to as junk food, including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder.

According to recent reports, however, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch.

Food is a key source of amino acids, nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains. Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them.

When you eat sulfur-rich foods, your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases. That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health. In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness, such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about.

In a recent development, as you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates, including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise.

According to recent reports, farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia. According to the Guinness Book of World Records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned latest husbands about their wives’ farts. The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “Despicable Me,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mishears his boss’s demand for a dart gun, instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy.

According to recent reports, but sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand, spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances, such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself.

Despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules.

These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves, and volcanic vents that can suffocate and kill you.

So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect.

It has been revealed that written by Brenda A. Wilson, Professor of Microbiology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

#214781. Scientists Discover Strange Dinosaur That Evolved To Eat Fruit

Scientists Discover Strange Dinosaur That Evolved To Eat Fruit

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A dinosaur’s resemblance to modern fruit-eating parrots offers clues to how prehistoric animals adapted as flowering plants transformed life on land.
  • According to recent reports, as flowering plants spread across the Cretaceous landscape, fruits became larger and more abundant, offering dinosaurs an entirely different source of food.
  • Recent findings suggest that the newly identified species, Infernogallus jamesi, is the first known dinosaur with anatomical adaptations specifically linked to fruit consumption.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A dinosaur’s resemblance to modern fruit-eating parrots offers clues to how prehistoric animals adapted as flowering plants transformed life on land.

According to recent reports, as flowering plants spread across the Cretaceous landscape, fruits became larger and more abundant, offering dinosaurs an entirely different source of food. Paleontologists have long struggled to understand how this transformation influenced dinosaur evolution. Now, the discovery of a turkey-sized dinosaur that lived alongside T. rex suggests that some dinosaurs developed remarkably sophisticated ways of eating fruit, much like parrots do today.

Recent findings suggest that the newly identified species, Infernogallus jamesi, is the first known dinosaur with anatomical adaptations specifically linked to fruit consumption. The discovery was made by researchers from Stony Brook University, the Royal Ontario Museum (ROM), and the North Dakota Geological Survey. Led by Dr. Gregory Funston, assistant professor in the Department of Anatomical Sciences at Stony Brook University, the study was published in Nature Communications.

It has been revealed that “We knew dinosaurs evolved to fill so many different roles in ecosystems in the Cretaceous, but we never expected to discover fruit-eating dinosaurs,” says Dr. Gregory Funston. “For more than 100 years, we didn’t know what the skulls of these animals looked like. Now, we know they were even weirder than we could have predicted.”.

According to recent reports, the dinosaur’s name, Infernogallus, means “hell chicken,” a reference to the Hell Creek Formation where its fossils were discovered. The formation stretches across Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Wyoming and preserves remains of familiar dinosaurs such as T. rex and Triceratops, which lived alongside Infernogallus. Its nearly complete skull, with the bones still connected, and partial skeleton are right now on display at the Royal Ontario Museum.

According to recent reports, despite descending from meat-eating dinosaurs, Infernogallus belonged to a group of toothless, feathered oviraptorosaurs known as caenagnathids. Weighing approximately 25 pounds (12 kilograms) as a fully grown adult, it was one of the smallest members of its group.

“It’s pretty rare for animals to become specialized for a diet of fruit, so when it happens, it comes with some remarkable adaptations,” says Dr. Thomas Dudgeon, Rebanks Postdoctoral Research Fellow at ROM and a co-author of the study. “The anatomy of Infernogallus is bizarre among dinosaurs, and we rapidly realized that we were dealing with something special.”.

Using CT scans to reconstruct the skull, the researchers noticed something unusual about the bones forming the roof of the mouth. These bones curved downward into the mouth, positioning certain chewing muscles horizontally rather than vertically. Instead of relying on the rigid, up-and-down bite characteristic of dinosaurs such as T. rex, Infernogallus could have moved its beak back and forth in a chewing motion similar to our own.

Sources indicate that forward-facing chewing muscles are uncommon in the animal kingdom, although they occur in mammals capable of complex chewing and in certain fruit-eating birds. The particular muscle arrangement identified in Infernogallus resembles that of the modern vulturine parrot (Psittrichas), suggesting that the dinosaur was adapted to processing soft food in its mouth rather than its gut. Its chewing motion appears to have been especially suited to separating the flesh of stone fruits from their hard central pits.

The finding also reveals an intriguing parallel in evolutionary history. As fruits became larger and more common, caenagnathids developed increasingly specialized chewing capabilities.

It has been revealed that fossilized fruits document how flowering plants gradually replaced cone-bearing plants as the dominant vegetation on land during the Cretaceous. By eating fruit, dinosaurs may have helped disperse seeds and influenced the evolution of flowering plants, fulfilling an ecological role that birds, reptiles, and small mammals play today.

“Complete remains of small dinosaurs like Infernogallus are very rare in the fossil record. The strange skull of Infernogallus is an exciting find because it reveals surprising insights into dinosaur evolution and feeding specialization,” states Dr. David Evans, chief curator of natural history and Temerty Chair in Vertebrate Paleontology at ROM and senior author of the paper. “This discovery shows that we still have a lot to learn about the world of T. rex, and about dinosaurs more generally.”.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery also contributes to an ongoing debate over whether dinosaurs were already in decline before their extinction. The specialized feeding behavior of Infernogallus suggests that the diversity of dinosaurs, and the ecological roles they occupied near the end of the Cretaceous, may have been greater than the fossil record has so far revealed.

Reference: “Fruit-eating adaptations in a Late Cretaceous oviraptorosaur (Theropoda)” by Gregory F. Funston, Thomas W. Dudgeon, D. Jade Simon, Danielle M. Dufault, Clint Boyd, Denver Fowler, Philip J. Currie and David C. Evans, 10 October 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78343-w.

In a recent development, sebnem Ece Eksi did a double take. Proteins typically studied in the brain were turning up in prostate cancer cells from high-risk patients. These proteins, called neuronal adhesion molecules, play a key role in the circuitry associated with memory.

The finding, made during her Ph.D. days at the University of Illinois Chicago, raised so many questions to which Eksi is still seeking answers. Now at the Oregon Health & Science University in Portland, Eksi has made it her lab’s goal to find out how nervous systems communicate with cancer. What were once two separate fields might be connected more closely than previously thought.

Sources indicate that “What we’re learning is that tumors are actively communicating with the nervous system,” Eksi indicates. “In a way, it makes sense to me that a growing tumor in our bodies, in an organ, would be immediately sensed and detected by the nervous system.”.

Eksi now plans to test an AI image-based recognition algorithm to identify nerve fibers in human patients. This is exciting, she says, because these nerves aren’t normally visible in patient tumors. But through biopsies, she hopes to map out and observe how the nervous system — which impacts sleep, cognition and pain — changes as cancer progresses. The implications are significant, she says. Could experts use the nervous system to detect cancer early? Can they improve patients’ quality of life?

In a recent development, “This field of cancer neuroscience can change all different stages of cancer diagnosis and treatments,” Eksi indicates. “It’s growing so quickly, the field itself.”.

Start by considering what you want to power during an emergency, like a refrigerator, a computer setup, or the entire house. Or, if you're camping or on a job site, consider the devices you want to power or recharge, such as power tools or camping gear like portable refrigerators.

Then consider the type of generator or power station you want. Fuel-based generators can run as long as you have enough fuel, but they’re loud and must be run outside because they emit potentially dangerous fumes. Power stations, on the other hand, run virtually silently and don’t emit fumes, so you can run them inside, making them great for city dwellers. They need to be recharged, but you can do that with AC power or a solar panel.

No matter what type you choose, it will cost several hundred dollars or more, so Black Friday and Cyber Monday are a good time to knock 20 to 40 percent off the regular price, including popular brands such as Jackery, Bluetti, EcoFlow, Generac, and Champion Power Equipment.

In a recent development, the lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Industry observers note that sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are right now scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen mentioned Sunday on CNN.

In a recent development, ​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A latest matter is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

In a recent development, "We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel.".

In a recent development, meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

Upcoming member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is at the moment the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Yian Yin seeks to understand the dynamics of science itself. The computational social scientist is particularly interested in how innovations happen and how they may be accelerated.

“I want to understand what the secret sources or recipes of success are,” claims Yin, of Cornell University.

He applied machine learning techniques to accepted and rejected research proposals to understand how scientists learn from failures. What he found was that scientists fail, and they fail often. Some switched gears after some rejections, but others who continued their research and incorporated feedback found success at a faster rate. Those who changed ideas or scrapped original proposals did not leverage a lot from their experience.

“A group that’s not only failing better and better,” Yin indicates, “is also failing faster and increasingly faster towards their eventual success.”.

Sources indicate that more recently, Yin has been investigating how generative AI is changing scientific publishing. Journals are receiving more AI-assisted submissions than ever before, which is leading the peer-review process to falter. More seemingly well-written papers that lack substance are getting through, he found. Coming up with large-scale solutions requires looking at the problem in a measurable way, Yin says.

“Considering both the technological and social side of scientific ecosystems would be something that’s really beneficial for the ongoing public debate and discussion about how we accelerate science in the age of artificial intelligence,” Yin indicates.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much.
  • When you’re shopping for a portable generator, there are a few important things to consider, including power, weight, and fuel type.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that generators come in all sizes, but when you need power for camping or tailgating, or to power tools when you’re too far from an outlet, a large one meant for home backup is just too much. Power stations are handy, but once they run out of power, they take a long time to recharge. That’s where a smaller-sized portable generator can really shine. So long as you have the fuel, they can keep running.

When you’re shopping for a portable generator, there are a few important things to consider, including power, weight, and fuel type. For portable power, models that output 2,000 to 5,000 watts will generally be simple enough to lift in and out of a truck, though some models that generate more are designed to be lightweight. Anything over 100 pounds starts to buck the idea of something being portable, even if it has wheels.

Industry observers note that fuel type matters, too. All generators run on gas, but dual-fuel models can also run on propane. The drawback is that propane delivers slightly less power output and shorter running time, but it runs a lot cleaner and is much less messy to deal with.

It has been revealed that if you’re powering sensitive electronics like digital equipment or TVs, you’ll also want to look for an inverter generator, which delivers more stable “cleaner” power that won’t damage your gear. They also run quieter than standard models. For these reasons, all of the picks on our list are inverter generators.

Sources indicate that keeping portability in mind, the models we cover in this story are all 7,500 watts and under. For the models that we tested, we based our methods on our experience using generators for backup power with and without transfer switches, on construction sites to run power tools and equipment, as well as running sound systems and lighting at outdoor events. We measured the sound levels of these generators idling with no load, and while running under load at two feet and 25 feet. We then used an oscilloscope to observe the sine wave of the alternating current generated by these machines, and a clamp meter to check voltage output.

Sources indicate that some examples of devices we used with large starting and running loads include a large air conditioner and a portable table saw. In one case, we even tested it paired to a solar inverter-charger. We evaluated these generators based on ease of starting, power response, sound levels, value, safety, and reliability to select the top performers.

The Honda EU2200i inverter generator has just about everything you want from a portable generator. It’s half the size and weight of comparable generators in its class; it’s very quiet and clean when operating; and it’s fully enclosed so you can quickly and easily transport it and move it around without worrying about it getting caught on anything.

It has been revealed that that enclosure is an vital feature, as it protects the inverter electronics and helps contain noise—the EU2200i is remarkably quiet. In testing, we measured sound levels of 68.9 decibels at the generator under no load. When we switched it to “eco” mode, which reduces engine speed when power isn’t called for, the sound was reduced to 76 decibels.

It has been revealed that when we used an oscilloscope to look at the sine wave of the current generated, the curves were smooth and symmetrical, an indicator of “clean” power. This remained true even when running heavy loads from devices like a table saw or an air conditioner.

Recent findings suggest that there are some nice design features, too. The vent on the gas cap closes so fumes or fuel cannot escape. You could breathe freely packing this in the passenger compartment of an SUV. Likewise, the power on/off switch doubles as a fuel shutoff, so it can’t be forgotten.

According to recent reports, lastly, the EU2200i has ports for parallel operation. With the correct cable kit, it connects to a second EU2200i to double the output to 4,400 starting and 3,600 running watts. The EU2200i is ideal for camping and other outdoor events where generator noise might be frowned on.

We like the GD400BN because it’s powerful, quiet, and portable at a reasonable price point. The interesting thing about this inverter generator is how much power it can deliver, yet it’s still as compact as similar generators that deliver half as much output. Even when running on lower-output propane as the fuel source, it can run up to 3,000 watts, which is considerable for a generator that only weighs 47 pounds.

Sources indicate that another plug or two would’ve been nice, however. Its single AC outlet limits you to plugging one power tool or appliance at a time, despite having enough output to power more than one device. It does have a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet for connecting to an RV, though, so that does make up for it a bit, but only if you have that need. The 1.1-gallon fuel tank is also a bit limiting regarding runtime for gasoline, but that’s easily overcome by using propane. For all intents and purposes, this is a very nice dual-fuel generator, and at a list price of $600, it comes at a reasonable price to boot.

The Wen DF360iX offers a considerable amount of utility for an affordable price. You have the option to run the generator on gasoline or propane with a running output of up to 2,900 watts. While propane delivers a bit less at 2,600 watts, that’s plenty of power for a job site or camping use and even enough electricity for small to midsize RVs.

According to recent reports, while this generator is fairly light at 49 pounds, it doesn’t cut back on ports, including a 30-amp port for direct connection to an RV. There are also two three-prong AC ports, a 12-volt DC receptacle, and two USB-A ports. Like most inverter generators, it produces less noise. This model is rated at around 65 decibels of noise at a quarter load, which is quiet enough that it shouldn’t bother the neighbors. There are some nice safety features, too, including auto-shutoff if the fuel runs too low and a carbon monoxide (CO) sensor that detects if dangerous levels are present.

Of course, with any generator in this price range (under $500), there are compromises. This model has a pretty small fuel tank—only 1.5 gallons—so you won’t be able to run this on gasoline for long periods (around five hours with a half-load) without having to stop and refill. You can mitigate this, however, by relying on a larger tank of propane. For example, a 20-pound tank should enable you to run it for up to 14 hours.

Recent findings suggest that GENERATOR SAFETYWhile not hard to run, generators present dangers, so you need to follow basic safety rules. Never operate them in a closed space, like a garage or shed. Exhaust gases contain carbon monoxide (CO), a lethal, odorless, colorless gas. Most manufacturers offer models that shut down when they detect carbon monoxide building up. Do not run a generator in a garage with the door open, or in front of the garage with the door open, because carbon monoxide can still get trapped and seep into the house. Run generators at least 20 feet away, including from windows and doors, with the exhaust blowing away from the house.

RV owners need a generator outfitted with at least a 120-volt, 30-amp outlet, but it also helps to have a decent amount of power to go with it, so that you can run things like a heater or an air conditioner. This model from Champion offers both, with the outlet and up to 3,500 running watts, which is enough to power a small- to medium-sized RV.

Recent findings suggest that it also offers great fuel flexibility. With a full 2.3-gallon fuel tank, it should be able to run for up to 14 hours, but it’s dual-fuel, so with a full 20-pound propane tank, this generator can supply 21 hours of uninterrupted power.

It has been revealed that in addition to being a solid companion for camping and RVing, this generator could serve as a useful tool in an emergency at home where power is needed. Using a manual transfer switch, you could power a few 120-volt circuits using the 30-amp connection. And the inverter will help to keep it running more quietly, which is helpful at home or the campground.

Recent findings suggest that one of our test editors picked up this generator when faced with a home emergency where he needed a generator with specific features, rapidly, and on a budget. A failed generator at a solar-powered off-grid cabin necessitated the quick acquisition, and, happily, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel Inverter Generator highlighted up on the doorstep in only two days.

Industry observers note that in about 15 minutes, with minimal assembly and after adding oil, the generator was connected to a propane cylinder by a hose and was running on the first cycle of the starter. Since then, it’s run steadily at 500 watts, up to 5,500 watts, at 240 volts (great for powering high-voltage appliances like dryers or water pumps), to charge a battery bank during the winter when sunlight wasn’t enough to get the job done.

This Pulsar puts out very clean power, too, with a claimed total harmonic distortion (THD) of less than 3 percent, which met the requirements of the solar inverter-charger it was paired with.

Using the inverter to monitor the current frequency, we found that it was indeed very stable with minimal variance, between 59.97 and 60.09 Hz. All things considered, the Pulsar 7,250-Watt Dual-Fuel is a good value for the specs, capacity, and features.

In a recent development, generac’s iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator is a great example of what we love about dual-fuel, inverter generators. This type of generator can deliver cleaner power than a standard model, meaning there’s less distortion in the electrical current frequency. That’s ideal for powering sensitive electronics, such as TVs, computer equipment, and smart household appliances. This is also a closed-frame inverter generator, which tends to be quieter; the iQ3800 is one of the quietest generators we’ve tested of this size.

We were very impressed with how easy the iQ3800 is to operate. The electric start and auto choke worked perfectly, taking only about four to five seconds, while the manual pull-start also fired up the generator with minimal effort. Switching between fuel types was also very simple to perform. Once running, you can view key information on an easy-to-read LED display that lists the total hours the machine has run, the fuel level for the gasoline tank (there’s no gauge for propane), and a load gauge that uses a bar graph to show power output level—knowing that helps to avoid overloading the generator.

In a recent development, the inverter technology might be the most important feature of the iQ3800. This generator has a total harmonic distortion (THD)—a level of variance in the current frequency—of less than 3 percent, which is very low. Essentially, anything with a screen or any smart device would be best powered using an inverter generator like the iQ3800. It’s an ideal generator to power RVs in campgrounds or off-grid, and a great option for emergency backup in urban areas.

Full Generac iQ3800 Portable Inverter Generator Review.

Recent findings suggest that these generators, sometimes called backup generators, are used to provide temporary power when and where it is needed. Portable is a relative term; some are more portable than others. While the smallest models can be picked up and carried, most have wheels and a handle to make transport easier. However, at 100 pounds or more, picking them up to load or move may take two people. Appliances, power tools, or other devices can be plugged directly into standard outlets on the generator’s front panel.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, many models have a twist-lock plug that can provide up to 240 volts and be used to power circuits in a home via a manual transfer switch. You may hear generators like these referred to as “open frame” generators, which simply means that the engine, fuel tank, and generator components are not enclosed in bodywork.

Though inverter-type generators are—like their standard cousins—typically portable, we group them separately because they’re significantly and technically different in terms of how they work.

Like most generators, inverter generators provide 120/240 volts of AC power. They generate AC current just like the others, but it’s then converted to DC (Direct Current), and then inverted back to AC. The conversion and inversion is controlled by circuitry which acts like a filter, flattens surges, and cleans up the sine wave (or oscillating wave) of the electrical current.

Typical generators have varying degrees of distortion in the sine wave of the alternating current. This isn’t usually an glitch for most electrical devices, though sensitive electronics like tablets, laptops, televisions, and other smart devices can be damaged by current distortion or surges. These devices will last longer with “clean” power and steady voltage. Because of that added complication, inverter generators can be significantly more expensive.

Standby generators are permanently installed and connected to a home. These may power selected, critical circuits during a power outage, or may provide power for the whole home. Standby generators have systems that monitor power supplied by a utility and start automatically in the event of an outage. Since they’re not portable or easily moved, we didn’t include any here.

Industry observers note that it’s important to know what you intend to power with a generator in order to choose the right size. Manufacturers list two figures for generators: starting watts and running watts. Starting watts include the initial surge required to start appliances or tools with powerful electric motors or compressors. Once started, these devices require far less power to run continuously.

Many manufacturers have a chart with estimated power requirements for common appliances and tools to help you figure out what you need. For a more precise measurement, you can also calculate the figure yourself by adding up the power consumption of specific appliances and adding them together.

It has been revealed that to calculate watts, multiply voltage (usually 120 volts) by the amps (amperage) required to run the appliance (usually found on a tag attached to the appliance). Do this for each item that the generator will power.

It has been revealed that most portable generators are powered by gasoline, the most commonly available fuel. However, when using generators for emergency power, their infrequent use presents some issues to consider.

According to recent reports, the first is that when massive, catastrophic storms hit and power outages last for days, gas stations may struggle to meet demand, resulting in long lines. The second issue has to do with the infrequent use of backup generators, which may sit for months to years between uses.

According to recent reports, gasoline sitting in a carburetor will slowly evaporate over time, leaving gummy deposits that can block fuel from getting through, making it difficult or even impossible to start your generator without servicing. You can avoid this by closing the fuel valve and letting the generator run until it stalls, using up the remaining fuel in the carburetor. Also, over time, gasoline can oxidize or become “stale,” losing combustibility. It may also absorb water, which can then corrode fuel tanks and other metal components in the fuel system. Starting a generator regularly, as well as treating fuel with a stabilizer, can help fight these issues.

Ethanol-free gasoline, available at some gas stations, is also less susceptible to degradation over time than standard 87-octane pump gas; however, it’s still a good idea to mix the fuel going into your generator with stabilizer.

Dual-fuel generators can run on gasoline or liquified petroleum gas (LPG), commonly known as propane. Switching between the fuels is simple, and you won’t be tied to the availability of one type of fuel.

A substantial advantage of propane is that it’s very stable when stored for long periods of time. It won’t go stale, and it won’t gum up carburetors from sitting. Plus, some homes that use propane for other purposes may already have large storage tanks on the premises, foregoing the need to make repeated trips out for fuel.

The downside to propane is that it creates fewer BTUs (British Thermal Units, a measurement of energy) than the same amount of gasoline. So, a generator running on propane will have slightly reduced starting and running watts. On the plus side, though, it will also run a little quieter than those that run on gasoline.

It has been revealed that while not as common, tri-fuel generators add an option to connect by natural gas. Some propane-powered generators can be converted to run on natural gas, as well. Like propane, natural gas can run cleaner and a little quieter. However, it also creates fewer BTUs than gasoline and propane, so it will also produce reduced starting and running watts.

Natural gas also requires a dedicated line for the generator, which most homes that have access to natural gas will not have, and thus will need to be professionally installed.

If you’re powering appliances, tools, or other devices by plugging them directly into the standard outlets on the generator, the answer is no. If the generator is being used to power circuits in your home, maybe. It’s always best to consult the operator’s manual, a licensed electrician, or your local building officials about township ordinances—some localities may have requirements that differ from the National Electrical Code (NEC).

Electrical circuits need to be grounded to operate devices safely, so that any current that shorts out or has a fault is directed to the ground, i.e., the actual, literal earth, so the user doesn’t become the conduit to “ground.”.

Sources indicate that there are two ways that generators are grounded: neutral-bonded and floating neutral. Neutral-bonded means the neutral wire is connected (i.e., bonded) to the generator frame. With a floating neutral, the neutral is not connected to the frame. In the latter case, the generator should be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a grounding rod driven into the ground.

Generators with ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlets, when used to power circuits in your home, require neutral switching and a manual transfer switch, and must be grounded by connecting the ground terminal to a ground rod driven into the soil. Neutral-switching transfer switches are also referred to as three-pole transfer switches.

There could be numerous reasons for difficulty starting a generator. The first things to check are whether or not there's any fuel in the tank, and if the fuel valve is turned open. Then, check for any obstructions in the air cleaner box. If that’s clean, move on to check that the engine has spark.

If your generator has sat for a long time without treated fuel, the carburetor may be clogged up and require cleaning—if you’re unfamiliar with any of these steps, it may be best to take it to a shop for service.

In an emergency, use what you can get, but as a general rule, 87 octane fuel will be fine—just don’t go lower than that.

As long as we’re talking fuel, it’s always best to use ethanol-free fuel in equipment with small gas engines—if that’s not possible, nothing more than 10-percent ethanol. Ethanol can attract moisture, which will then separate and settle in the gas tank or carburetor, where it can corrode and clog the fuel system. For this reason, it’s also a good idea to treat gas with a fuel stabilizer.

Much like your lawn mower, generators need regular maintenance. However, since they often see less use, maintenance intervals tend to be farther apart. Typical maintenance would include changing oil, checking the air filter and changing it if needed, changing the fuel filter if so equipped, and checking the spark plug.

The best source of specific maintenance and troubleshooting information for your generator is the owner’s manual.

Industry News: Biden: ‘Hard to take’ as Pelosi, Schumer turned on him in 2024

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that president Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug.
  • Industry observers note that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir.
  • Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that president Joe Biden, Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., arrive for The CHIPS and Science Act of 2022 bill signing at the White House, on Aug. 9, 2022. In his latest memoir, Biden stated he was disappointed when Pelosi and Schumer urged him to drop out of the presidential race in 2024. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that in conversations with Democratic strategists in recent months, I heard a strikingly similar sentiment when the topic turned to Joe Biden’s forthcoming memoir. The consensus view, even among some who’d worked for the former president, was that if he did anything other than accept some responsibility for his role in Donald Trump’s return to the White House, they didn’t have much appetite to hear what he had to say about anything else.

Spoiler alert: Biden offers only a full-throated defense of his decision to seek reelection in 2024, and expresses deep disappointment over what he casts as a disloyal pressure campaign orchestrated by party leaders to force him out of the presidential race despite what he cites as his successes in the office.

But while his perspective on the climactic moment of his political career will be the most scrutinized portion of Biden’s new book, “Promise Me, America” seems primarily intended to offer the former president a platform he has otherwise not had since leaving office: to catalog what he sees as his historic achievements and offer his perspective on how he wrestled with the major issues of our time.

In a recent development, it’s often noted that the only thing better than being president is being a former president. That has hardly been the case for Biden in the nearly 22 months since he left the White House, especially as he’s endured what his son Hunter has described as “debilitating” physical pain following a cancer diagnosis last March.

But where “Thanks, Obama” became a popular mantra nearly a decade ago for Democrats seeking to defend and celebrate the 44th president’s record in contrast with the first Trump administration, no such widespread nostalgia has emerged around Biden, as the party is loath to revisit the trauma of the summer of 2024.

The sheer length of his latest book — more than 400 pages — seems an implicit acknowledgment that presenting a positive portrait of Biden’s single term in office is largely to be a solitary effort. Over 15 chapters, Biden offers sometimes mechanical descriptions of specific policies and their impact, but also new details of the sausage-making required to pass major initiatives like the Inflation Reduction Act. That legislation, he writes, was revived thanks in part to an Italian dinner hosted by Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo to make peace between West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin III and White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain.

Biden writes in sweeping terms about other accomplishments like responding to the COVID-19 crisis he inherited, calling his administration’s work “one of the most monumental achievements in public health history.” He repeatedly defends his frequent efforts to warn Americans about the need to safeguard our democracy even as critics in the press and his own party suggested he focus more on economic concerns.

According to recent reports, supporting Ukraine in its war against Russia gets the most extensive treatment of any single issue in the book, including a detailed account of Biden’s clandestine trip to Kyiv in February 2023. And the former Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman takes great effort to delve into the complexity of the U.S.-China relationship and his relationship with President Xi Jinping, while asserting that Taiwan “will likely be the most crucial foreign policy challenge in the world over the next generation.”.

According to recent reports, recurring throughout the book are expressions of optimism that under his administration, Washington was beginning to work again like it was supposed to, that America’s global leadership was being restored through its alliances, and that he was tackling problems that previous presidents had sidestepped. And in offering this comprehensive presentation of his record, Biden also offers his primary rationale for running again.

“We had accomplished so much —  I wanted to finish the job. And yes: I believed I was the best person to do it,” he states. “I was the only person who had ever beaten Donald Trump. And I felt I was the best person to do it again.”.

Recent findings suggest that one of Biden’s top advisers put it to me a different way in the months leading up to his decision to seek another term. “He has been running for president for 50 years. And the idea that he would actually be president and stop running for president is almost laughably preposterous.”.

The biggest question, of course, was his age, something Biden, who was 81 when he dropped out of the race, asserts he gave serious consideration.

“I knew better than anyone how old I was. I knew what I was —  and wasn’t —  capable of doing. I carefully monitored how I was meeting the demands of the job. And there is not a single example of me failing to handle my responsibilities,” he writes.

The June 27 debate, of course, created a very different perception, as Biden acknowledges that his flubbed comment that “we finally beat Medicare” was to become “Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job.” But he tries to argue it was no different than the poor showings of previous incumbent presidents, including President Barack Obama, in their first debates.

Recent findings suggest that “The difference was that every other president was given the chance to redeem themselves in a second debate. As it turned out, that chance would not be available to me,” Biden writes.

He argues the response he was seeing from voters at his public events after the debate didn’t justify the panicked response of elected Democrats in Washington, and that public polling highlighted only minor slippage after the debate, until a steady drumbeat of elected Democrats publicly began calling for him to step aside.

According to recent reports, describing separate visits from former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., and then-Senate Majority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., personally urging him to step aside, he notes there was a “yawning gap between what I was seeing with Democratic voters and what I was hearing from the Democratic leadership in Washington.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I have to admit it was personally hard to take so many old friends turning on me,” Biden says. “I told Schumer he had a lot of gumption (I may have stated it differently at the time), coming to my home and telling me to get out of the race. Loyalty matters to me. If I give you my word, I stick with you. If I say I’m with you, I’m with you to the end.”.

At one point, Biden seems to reflect some resentment that some of the Democrats who would ultimately call on him to drop out of the race had themselves been too afraid to challenge him in the first place, saying: “Anyone who was scared off from running has no business being president.” While there was a constant narrative about the weakness of his candidacy, Biden acknowledges, the lack of a serious challenger was in fact a sign of his strength.

“I had it on good authority that several big names in Democratic politics had looked at running. They held meetings and took polls and talked to donors and to potential staff. If they thought I was weak or vulnerable, they would have taken their shot. But they didn’t,” he writes.

According to recent reports, biden’s defiant tone, and his insistence that the lack of party unity was a greater threat to his continued candidacy than his own performance, may be dismissed by Democrats who don’t want to revisit this difficult chapter. But as Schumer and other Democratic leaders are now facing their own internal challenges, “Promise Me, America” may also serve as a cautionary note for an ambitious crop of potential candidates hoping to reclaim the presidency in 2028.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that in an increasingly fire-prone western North America, Jennifer Grenz, an ecologist and member of the Lytton First Nation, looks at fire with a holistic eye. She considers her work with landscapes recovering from catastrophic wildfire to be “deliberately unfocused,” spanning soil microbial ecology, restoration ecology, invasion biology and historical biology.

Grenz analyzes historical ecological records, like how Indigenous people have shaped and cared for ecosystems over time, to paint a comprehensive picture. “I’m interested in how those histories leave ecological legacies and hints of the stewardship of the past,” says Grenz, who leads the Indigenous Ecology Lab at the University of British Columbia in Canada. “What changed on the land that made it more vulnerable?”.

Grenz spends time with many kinds of specialists, such as archaeologists, anthropologists and Indigenous elders who provide oral histories.

Moving forward, her lab will examine ecology below ground, including soil, microbial communities and root networks. The goal is to understand the role of underground ecology in critical topics like carbon sequestration, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management.

Sources indicate that “My motivation is in our interior Salish Territories in the southern interior of British Columbia, where my ancestors rest and where my people are,” Grenz claims. “The responsibility I feel to them and to our Tmícw, which means our lands, [is] to not take us back to the past, but to show that we have the deep knowledge to help us move forward.”.
