#214734. Ice baths don’t help your muscles recover after a workout any better than heat-based methods, according to a new study

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1008 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Ice baths don’t help your muscles recover after a workout any better than heat-based methods, according to a new study

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1008 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite the popularity of ice baths for post-workout recovery, upcoming research finds that cold-water immersion helps restore muscle strength no better than heat-based methods.
  • Enduring a freezing ice bath after a hard workout feels like a steep price to pay for better muscle recovery.
  • In a recent development, for this research project, forty people wrecked one thigh muscle on purpose.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite the popularity of ice baths for post-workout recovery, upcoming research finds that cold-water immersion helps restore muscle strength no better than heat-based methods.

Enduring a freezing ice bath after a hard workout feels like a steep price to pay for better muscle recovery. Now, results from a new study show that cold-water immersion restored strength no faster than sitting in a chair with a hot towel around your neck.

In a recent development, for this research project, forty people wrecked one thigh muscle on purpose. They then spent 15 to 30 minutes in cold water, hot water, hot air, or an ordinary room. Three days later, their strength had come back at the same pace in every group.

The hot water did change the body in ways the ice bath didn’t. Blood markers of muscle damage settled faster after a hot bath, and a protective protein rose more.

Those changes never showed up as extra strength or less soreness. So, for now, the finding is that heat and cold are different, not that either one is better.

Freya Bayne, a lecturer in sport and exercise science at the University of East London, led the study. Her co-authors came from London South Bank University, Maastricht University, and the University of Montpellier, among others.

Each person got one session of one treatment, and the follow-up stopped at 72 hours, so the results say nothing about weeks of regular ice baths.

“Cold-water immersion remains one of the most popular recovery strategies used by athletes and recreational exercisers alike,” Bayne said.

“Our findings suggest that heat-based recovery methods produce different physiological responses following strenuous exercise, particularly in relation to markers associated with cellular protection and muscle repair.”.

The volunteers were 40 adults, 31 of them men, averaging 26 years old, who already lifted weights three to five hours a week.

Each one sat at a machine that forced the dominant knee to bend while the thigh muscle fought it, 210 times in all. Contractions like that are what make muscles sore a day or two later.

Right after the session, the thigh could push with about 36 percent less force than before. That loss is what the recovery treatments were meant to undo.

Each person was assigned at random to one of four treatments, ten to a group. One group sat chest-deep in water at 108°F (42°C) for 30 minutes, and another sat in an ice bath at 48°F (9°C) for 15 minutes.

A third sat in a room heated to 86°F (30°C) for 30 minutes, and the last sat in a room at 64°F (18°C) in their gym clothes.

Everyone came back at 24, 48, and 72 hours to push against the machine again. They also gave blood and rated their pain and soreness.

By 72 hours, the hot water, hot air, and plain room groups had all recovered about 88 to 90 percent of their starting strength. The cold water group was at about 82 percent.

The gap between cold water and the rest looks like something, but with ten people per group the uncertainty around it is wide. The statistics could not separate any group from any other.

The authors wrote that the pattern fits other recent work suggesting cold can slow the signals that rebuild muscle, while stopping short of calling it a result.

Industry observers note that three things in the blood told a different story from the strength test. One was a protein called creatine kinase, which leaks out of damaged muscle fibers.

It was back to normal 48 hours after the hot bath and 72 hours after hot air or a plain room. After the cold bath, it was still about 25 percent above normal at 72 hours.

In a recent development, the second was heat shock protein 72, a protein that cells make under stress to protect and repair themselves. Right after the treatment, the hot water group’s level was more than three times its start. The cold water group’s was about one and a half times.

The third, an immune messenger called interleukin-6, spiked highest after the hot bath and then dropped fastest, back to near normal within a day.

According to recent reports, only the hot bath warmed the muscle itself, from 98°F to 102°F (36.6°C to 38.8°C). The cold bath cooled it to 93°F (34°C).

Pain and soreness rose in every group by the next day and were still up at 72 hours. No treatment brought them back to the starting point. The hot air group reported the most pain on days one and two and the most fatigue on days two and three.

Cold water held soreness down on the first day, but it climbed on the second before easing on the third.

“It is important to recognize that these responses did not result in significantly greater recovery of muscle strength or lower levels of soreness over the following 72 hours,” Bayne remarked.

The study tested a single session of each treatment, and the authors said one session may not capture what repeated use does.

The team didn’t track what the volunteers ate, and only asked them to state their first day’s meals. Soreness ratings were filled in online, and only 29 of the 40 people completed every one.

Recent findings suggest that with nine women among 40 people, the team couldn’t ask whether men and women respond differently to heat and cold. And the blood marker for muscle damage is an indirect one, since no muscle tissue was sampled.

Bayne’s team wants larger groups, repeated exposures, and tests of timing and dose. “Further research is needed to understand whether repeated exposure to heat-based recovery strategies might produce longer-term benefits,” she stated.

Until that work is done, heat changes the blood in ways cold does not, and the strength tests show no difference in recovery between them.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Thermal Biology.

A new AI tool could help fight online wildlife trafficking

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have developed a way to recognize elephant ivory, pangolin scales, and tiger claws in photographs to help investigators flag suspicious online listings.
  • A latest AI tool can identify elephant, pangolin, and tiger products in photographs, even among similar-looking everyday objects.
  • Tests suggest it could help investigators sift through online listings and decide which items deserve closer inspection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have developed a way to recognize elephant ivory, pangolin scales, and tiger claws in photographs to help investigators flag suspicious online listings.

A latest AI tool can identify elephant, pangolin, and tiger products in photographs, even among similar-looking everyday objects.

Tests suggest it could help investigators sift through online listings and decide which items deserve closer inspection.

The research was led by Enrico Di Minin at the University of Helsinki. Lead author Ritwik Kulkarni worked with the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) on the image library and prototype.

Wildlife products change appearance as they become jewelry, ornaments, or medicines. A photograph may show a carved bracelet, loose scales, or a claw, with few clues about its origin.

Illegal and unsustainable trade contributes to wildlife declines. Tracking it online means reviewing large numbers of photographs across shopping sites and social media, often with limited staff.

“Identifying illegal wildlife products, such as elephant ivory, using AI was one of the grand challenges we were facing,” Di Minin remarked.

“These new tools offer novel opportunities for real-time monitoring of online illegal trade in ivory, pangolin scales, and tiger claws for enforcement purposes.”.

The researchers assembled 39,941 images collected through IFAW’s monitoring work in China between 2008 and 2023.

Industry observers note that sources included online advertisements, market inspections, publicly reported seizures, and image searches. This gave the team examples of products as they actually appeared in trade-related photographs.

Sources indicate that the library also included objects that could fool a reviewer. Jade bracelets resembled ivory bracelets, while slices of herbal medicine looked like pangolin scales.

Two experienced IFAW analysts reviewed the labels and resolved disagreements. Objects were also marked with boxes, teaching the model where to look within each photograph.

Recent findings suggest that that mattered for crowded product displays and collages. The system needed to locate a suspicious item even when other objects appeared beside it.

It has been revealed that the team compared models trained separately for each target group with a model trained on all three. The combined approach performed best overall.

“The best model achieved an overall accuracy of 84% and exceeded 90% accuracy for tiger and pangolin products,” Kulkarni stated.

The paper gives the figures as 93.6% for pangolin products and 90.3% for tiger products. Elephant products proved harder, with an accuracy of 71.1%.

Ivory carvings can resemble objects made from bone or resin. The researchers also noted that models may sometimes rely on surrounding visual clues instead of the object’s identifying features.

“When integrated into a research prototype smartphone application and evaluated independently, the tool reached 91.3% accuracy in practical screening tests, highlighting the potential of automated image analysis to help prioritise suspect content for human review,” Kulkarni explained.

The app was assessed using 138 additional images, separately from the initial model tests.

Sources indicate that the prototype lets consumers choose an existing photograph or take a fresh one. It then returns a prediction, with boxes marking the objects it has detected.

Recent findings suggest that an investigator reviewing online advertisements could submit saved images. During a market inspection, an officer could photograph an item for an initial assessment.

“For these technologies to make a meaningful contribution to conservation, we need to make them accessible and usable by the people working on the ground,” Kulkarni said.

“Our prototype demonstrates how we can bridge the gap between AI research and practical conservation applications. An app built on it could help, for example, conservation organizations and authorities.”.

Industry observers note that owners can also give feedback on whether the labels and boxes are correct. That provides a way to record mistakes and improve later versions.

A photograph cannot settle whether a sale is illegal. A flagged image gives investigators something to examine, while qualified authorities remain responsible for legal decisions.

According to recent reports, errors create different problems. False alarms send reviewers toward ordinary goods, while missed detections can leave suspicious listings unnoticed.

Recent findings suggest that the aim is to help people decide where to spend their time. Specialists would still need to examine the item, the listing, and any other relevant evidence.

Recent findings suggest that the reported results measure image-recognition performance. They do not show how many illegal sales the tool would prevent or how much it would reduce pressure on wildlife populations.

The researchers plan to improve accuracy, add more species and products, and explore pilots with conservation organizations and online platforms.

They also want secure, ethical procedures for referring suspected cases to authorities.

Continued training will matter because products and their presentation change. A system built from past photographs needs updating as latest examples enter the market.

The paper also suggests combining images with information from listing text. That could help when a photograph alone leaves too much uncertainty.

“We are excited to see this research translate into a practical screening tool for combating illegal online wildlife trade,” said Lionel Hachemin, IFAW’s Wildlife Crime Program Director.

Industry observers note that “This study demonstrates what’s possible when conservation organizations and researchers join forces. We see this as a practical step toward turning the tide on illegal wildlife trade online.”.

The study is published in the journal Conservation Biology.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that even the best-laid prepares can require a bit of luck to execute.
  • In a recent development, “I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy.
  • The work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that even the best-laid prepares can require a bit of luck to execute. During the solar eclipse of Aug. 12, 2026, in which parts of Iceland, Portugal, and Spain experienced totality, much of western Europe enjoyed a substantial partial eclipse. Astrophotographer Alexandre Tournay set up near Brussels to capture the Moon crossing the disk — as well as a transit of another kind.

In a recent development, “I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy. “Against the odds, one did, passing across the partially eclipsed solar disk with its contrail trailing behind it.” Flight tracking data allowed him to pinpoint the flight: Cargolux 5933, a Boeing 747 freighter from Mexico City bound for Luxembourg.

The work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames. That process brings out the roiling details in the Sun’s chromosphere, but would oversharpen the edges of the airplane and Moon. So Tournay blended a 1,000-frame stack of the Sun with a single frame that preserved the silhouettes and froze their motion against the disk.

He named the resulting image “Phaethon’s Flight” after the boy in Greek mythology who journeyed east to prove that his father was Helios, the Sun god. Phaethon convinced Helios to let him drive his Sun-bearing chariot across the sky, but was unable to control the horses. He blazed an erratic path that brought climatic extremes to Earth — freezing cold and scorching heat — before Zeus intervened and struck him down dead.

Industry observers note that “There’s something fascinating about being able to photograph, with modern instruments, a celestial phenomenon that our ancestors could only understand and describe through mythology,” states Tournay. “And then, by pure chance, to have a flying machine cross the Sun at that exact moment, almost as though a modern-day chariot were dragging the eclipse behind it across the sky, made the story of Phaethon feel like a perfect fit. Seeing that plane cross the eclipsed Sun, I can almost hear the ancients screaming, ‘See?! I told you it was Phaethon!’ ”.

Mark Zastrow is Editor-in-Chief of Astronomy magazine. He holds masters degrees in astronomy and science journalism and has over a decade of experience covering science in the U.S. and in Asia.

#214730. The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1890 w)

The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a newly introduced scale measuring masculinity.
  • For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a newly introduced scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

Industry observers note that but giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” indicates Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health complications — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

Industry observers note that the first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

That thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

Inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”.

The higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

It has been revealed that but almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”.

Yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson notes. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

Sources indicate that englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

He and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

In a recent development, but the study also showed that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Sources indicate that then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their upcoming masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work shows. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott notes. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”.

“I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott says. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”.

Most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he notes. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”.

Fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher says. “And he’s been struggling.”.

Perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher says. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

It has been revealed that so for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales currently in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a fresh masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

Movember Institute of Men’s Health.

All the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher states. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he says.

A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”.

Researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, says psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a fresh masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Recent findings suggest that theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”.

According to recent reports, such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher states. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis says. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

However the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”.

#214728. Benjamin Franklin mocked the bald eagle in a 1784 letter and praised the turkey, but never asked for it to be the national bird

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1068 w)

Benjamin Franklin mocked the bald eagle in a 1784 letter and praised the turkey, but never asked for it to be the national bird

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1068 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The letter, never mailed to his daughter, was not published in full in English until 1817.
  • A popular Thanksgiving story holds that Benjamin Franklin wanted the turkey, not the bald eagle, to be the national bird of the United States.
  • Sources indicate that the story traces back to a letter dated January 26, 1784, and addressed to his daughter, Sarah Bache.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The letter, never mailed to his daughter, was not published in full in English until 1817. The bald eagle became the national bird by law only in 2024.

A popular Thanksgiving story holds that Benjamin Franklin wanted the turkey, not the bald eagle, to be the national bird of the United States. It is a good story, but it is not what Franklin actually wrote.

Sources indicate that the story traces back to a letter dated January 26, 1784, and addressed to his daughter, Sarah Bache. In it, he poked fun at the eagle on the badge of the Society of the Cincinnati and mentioned a few kind words about the turkey. In that letter, he never proposes the turkey as a national symbol.

According to the editors of his papers, Franklin never even sent the letter to his daughter. And the bald eagle itself was officially designated the national bird by law only in 2024, more than two centuries later.

It has been revealed that when Franklin wrote the letter, the bald eagle was already on the Great Seal of the United States. It had been adopted for the seal on June 20, 1782.

In the winter of 1783 to 1784, Franklin, the American minister, was too ill to travel and isolated at Passy, in France, according to the editors of his papers.

On January 26, he saw the founding document of the Society of the Cincinnati, a hereditary order of American army officers. John Paul Jones had sent it to him along with a pamphlet attacking the society.

The letter that Franklin wrote that same day was, in the view of the editors of The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, a satire meant as a public essay.

Addressing it to his daughter, with whom, the editors note, he never corresponded about politics, made it look like a private note.

In a recent development, he took aim at the idea of passing honors down to children. He objected to “an order of hereditary Knights, in direct opposition to the solemnly declared sense of their country.”.

According to recent reports, he even did the math. In nine generations, he wrote, a member’s share in his descendant would be “but a 512th part.”.

The birds come up near the end, when Franklin turns to the society’s badges, which had been made in France. “To me they seem tolerably done; but all such things are criticised,” he wrote.

Some critics, he reported, disliked the Latin mottos. “Others object to the bald eagle, as looking too much like a Dindon or turkey,” he wrote, using the French word for turkey.

Sources indicate that then Franklin gave his own opinion. “For my own part I wish the bald eagle had not been chosen as the representative of our country,” he wrote. “He is a bird of bad moral character. He does not get his living honestly.”.

Sources indicate that he described the eagle sitting on a dead tree, “too lazy to fish for himself,” while it watched another bird, which he called the fishing hawk. When that bird caught a fish and carried it toward its nest, he wrote, the eagle “pursues him, and takes it from him.”.

He went further. “Besides he is a rank coward,” Franklin wrote. The “little king bird not bigger than a sparrow attacks him boldly and drives him out of the district.”.

It has been revealed that only then does Franklin praise the turkey. He wrote that he was “not displeased” that the figure on the badge was not recognizable as a bald eagle and looked more like a turkey.

It has been revealed that “For in truth, the turkey is in comparison a much more respectable bird, and withal a true original native of America,” he wrote. Eagles, he noted, “have been found in all countries, but the turkey was peculiar to ours.”.

It has been revealed that he did not spare the turkey entirely. He called it “a little vain and silly,” though “not the worse emblem for that,” and “a bird of courage” that would attack a grenadier of the British guards who dared to invade its farmyard “with a red coat on.”.

Sources indicate that nowhere in the letter does Franklin ask for the turkey to replace the eagle on the seal or anywhere else. The comparison is part of a joke about a badge.

According to the editors of his papers, Franklin showed the letter only to his grandsons before sending it, around March 1784, to the abbé Morellet in France to translate it into French. Morellet advised against publishing it. Franklin agreed and promised it would not appear while he was alive.

Recent findings suggest that A partial French translation came out in Paris in 1790, months after Franklin’s death. The full English text was not published until 1817, when William Temple Franklin included it in his edition of Franklin’s writings.

In other words, the letter that so many people now quote was almost unknown in Franklin’s lifetime.

Sources indicate that the bald eagle’s official title came with a bill that Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota introduced on June 20, 2024, exactly 242 years after the eagle was adopted for the Great Seal.

Sources indicate that the Senate passed it by unanimous consent in July 2024, and the House approved it by voice vote on December 16, 2024. It was signed into law on December 23, 2024, as Public Law 118-206.

The law adds a new section to the U.S. Code. It reads: “The bald eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) is the national bird.”.

In its findings, Congress noted that the bald eagle is unique to North America and that federal, state and local governments, nonprofit groups and individuals had all contributed to its recovery.

Even so, eagles still face problems, including the lead poisoning that is common in eagles.

The turkey’s history with people goes back much further than Franklin. Scientists have found that turkeys were domesticated at least 1,500 years ago.

The information was obtained from Benjamin Franklin’s letter to Sarah Bache of January 26, 1784, as published by the National Archives in Founders Online from The Papers of Benjamin Franklin, the record of S.4610 on Congress.gov, and the enrolled text of the bill published by the U.S. Government Publishing Office.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 24: A Super Beaver Moon occults the Pleiades.

The distant ice giant Uranus reaches opposition tonight at 6 P.M. EST. Opposition is the best time to view a planet in our sky, and it’s visible roughly from dusk until dawn. Because Uranus is faint — magnitude 5.6 — you’ll want to give it a few hours after sunset to climb away from both light pollution and turbulent air near the horizon. Around 10 P.M. local time, you’ll find Uranus midway between the bright star Aldebaran and the Pleiades star cluster in Taurus the Bull, about 60° above the southeastern horizon. It sits some 1.5° south of 4th-magnitude 37 Tauri.

Although Uranus can be visible to the naked eye under clear, dark conditions, the bright waning Moon is nearby, so pull out binoculars or a telescope to view the far-off planet tonight. Once you land on its location, look for a “flat,” grayish-colored star. Uranus’ disk spans 4”, so you will likely be able to tell it is circular, rather than a pinpoint of light like any background stars.

#214726. Industry News: The biggest concern about toddler screen time may be what children are missing

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1564 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The biggest concern about toddler screen time may be what children are missing

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many toddlers use screens daily, potentially missing valuable opportunities to play, talk, and learn through real human interaction.
  • It has been revealed that at 18 months, children are learning to name things, put words together and make sense of the world around them.
  • In Hungary, researchers found that 49% of children around this age used screens every day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many toddlers use screens daily, potentially missing valuable opportunities to play, talk, and learn through real human interaction.

It has been revealed that at 18 months, children are learning to name things, put words together and make sense of the world around them. Many are also becoming quite familiar with television and smartphones.

In Hungary, researchers found that 49% of children around this age used screens every day.

There has been plenty of debate over how much screen time is appropriate for young children. A latest review, however, looks at a different side of the problem.

How much time is left for talking, playing and being with other people?

Krisztina Kopcsó, a researcher at the HCSO Institute for Quantitative Population and Economic Research in Budapest, led the review.

Kopcsó and her colleagues drew on data from a Hungarian national survey and research from around the world published since 2015.

Among the authors was Ákos Pogány from the Department of Ethology at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE).

Recent findings suggest that “Young children learn primarily through actively exploring the world and interacting with others, rather than through screens. One of the greatest risks of introducing digital devices too early is that their use takes time away from precisely these essential experiences,” Pogány mentioned.

According to recent reports, screen exposure before age two is discouraged by the World Health Organization and the American Academy of Pediatrics. Video chatting with distant family members is treated as an exception.

Recent findings suggest that A more restrictive position has been adopted in France. Complete screen abstinence until age three was recommended by an expert committee appointed by the French President.

A recent Hungarian expert guideline also recommends avoiding screens before age three.

Despite these recommendations, early screen exposure is widespread. A 2022 meta-analysis included 63 studies and more than 89,000 children.

Only 24.7% of children under two were found to meet the guideline of no screen use.

Sources indicate that in the United States, children under two averaged 63 minutes of screen media per day in 2024. These data were reported in the Common Sense Media census. By age two, 40% of children owned their own tablet.

Objective measurements were used in the Australian EUiLO cohort, described by Brushe and colleagues in 2023. A child-worn device recorded electronic noise for 16 hours on a typical day.

It has been revealed that families with lower educational attainment were oversampled among the 207 children. At 24 months, no screen exposure was recorded for only 2.4% of them.

Mean daily exposure in that cohort was 76.1 minutes at 6 months and 148.3 minutes at 24 months.

The Hungarian data were obtained from the Cohort ’18 Growing Up in Hungary panel study. A representative sample was recruited during pregnancy.

Maternal reports for 2,569 children were collected in 2019 and 2020 and analyzed by Kopcsó and colleagues in 2024. The children were aged between 15 and 23 months.

The database was weighted for maternal age, education, parity and marital status.

Daily screen exposure was reported for 49% of the children. More than one hour of exposure on a typical day was recorded for 37.5%. No exposure was reported for 14%.

Among daily users, mean screen time on a typical day was 122.5 minutes.

Most children were cared for at home. Only 6.7% attended formal childcare at the time of the survey.

Television viewing was identified as the most frequent screen activity. It was watched every day by 43.6% of the children.

Videos on mobile devices were watched daily by 21.2% of children. Active touchscreen use on a daily basis was reported for 18.7%.

Industry observers note that higher screen time was observed in lower-income households and among children of less educated mothers. Both gradients were statistically significant in the 2024 analysis.

In a recent development, A similar gradient was reported in a 2024 German study of 3,035 children by Paulus and colleagues. Parents there described using screens when time was short.

The contexts of screen use were also recorded in the Cohort ’18 survey.

Screen use while having fun with the child was reported by 62.1% of mothers.

Screens were allowed during household chores by 53.5%. Use for perceived developmental purposes was reported by 52.8%.

Background television was reported as a regular practice in 31.4% of families. It was rare or absent in 39.1%. The mother’s own relaxation was cited as a reason by 13.9%.

In Hungary, 19.6% of toddlers watched screens during meals, and 12.4% used them while falling asleep.

Children who spent more time with screens were read to and played with slightly less often, even after accounting for family income and mothers’ education.

However, busy parents may have less time for these activities, regardless of screen use.

A 2017 study linked screen use during more daily routines to delays in social and emotional development.

Another study in 2018 found that children who spent less time with screens at age two had better self-control at age four.

Apps and streaming content for babies are often marketed as educational.

A 2021 meta-analysis published in Child Development examined how well young children learn from videos compared with real-life demonstrations. Children aged 0 to 6 were included.

Less learning was found from video than from equivalent live demonstrations, and the gap narrowed with age.

Word learning from video was supported by adult co-viewing in a 2018 study by Strouse and colleagues.

It has been revealed that video chat was examined by Myers and colleagues in 2017 and by McClure and colleagues in 2018. Reciprocal interaction and joint attention cues are preserved in that format.

Screens were used to soothe or distract the child by 43% of Hungarian mothers. Frequent reliance on this strategy may reduce chances to practice self-regulation, the authors wrote.

Reciprocal associations between device use for calming and emotional reactivity were reported in a 2023 JAMA Pediatrics study.

Recent findings suggest that children aged 3 to 5 were followed. Similar associations were reported by Konok and colleagues at ELTE in 2024.

Autoplay, infinite scrolling and algorithmic recommendations are listed in the review as persuasive design features. Rapid cuts and high visual salience may also place heavy demands on immature attention.

A parent’s phone can interrupt even the simplest moments with a child. In 2018, researchers McDaniel and Radesky used the term technoference to describe these interruptions.

Studies conducted in restaurants and public places in the United States and Israel found that parents paid less attention to their children while using phones.

Some even responded rather sharply when their children sought their attention.

A 2015 study found that just hearing a phone notification was enough to distract someone, even if they ignored it.

Sources indicate that babies seem to notice these interruptions, too. In a 2018 study, infants whose mothers frequently used phones had a harder time returning to a happy mood, even after their mothers put the devices away.

In the French ELFE cohort, mean daily screen time at age two was 49 minutes in 2013, among 12,099 children.

Television exposure during family meals at age two was associated with poorer expressive language.

Less advanced general cognitive development was found at age 3.5, Yang and colleagues reported in 2024. Overall screen time was not the factor identified.

Earth.com has previously covered how a parent’s own phone use relates to vocabulary growth. The role of eye contact in infant language learning has also been reported.

A harm-reduction approach to infant media use was proposed by Heller in Infant Behavior and Development in 2021.

Age-appropriate limits combined with harm-reduction strategies are recommended in the review.

It has been revealed that background and parallel media use during caregiving routines and play should be reduced. Screen exposure during meals and before bedtime should be avoided.

Caregiver co-use is prioritized when screens are introduced in the second or third year.

Information could be provided to expecting parents through obstetric, prenatal and primary care services. Complaints about the no-screens-before-two rule have also been reported by parents.

Sources indicate that the European Union has rules to keep children safe online. Article 28 of its Digital Services Act focuses specifically on protecting young owners.

On July 14, 2025, the European Commission also issued guidelines addressing features that could make it difficult for children to stop using digital platforms.

However, these measures do not specifically address the needs of babies and toddlers.

The authors argue that keeping children safe from the potential harms of digital media should not be the responsibility of parents alone.

Reducing screen time sounds like a sensible idea, but researchers still have much to learn about its benefits for very young children.

A 2025 review of experiments involving preschoolers found that programs teaching parents about screen habits helped reduce children’s screen use.

Industry observers note that few studies, however, have tested similar approaches in children under two. Even fewer have followed children long enough to see whether their language skills, sleep or ability to manage emotions improved.

Future studies could test whether replacing screen time with play and reading improves language development in children under two.

For young children, what they do after the screen goes off may be just as important as switching it off in the first place.

The review was published in the journal Biologia Futura.

Garages and unfinished basements are often poorly insulated, making them prone to extreme cold in fall and winter. A garage heater can turn this typically frigid space into a warm, practical area for woodworking projects, vehicle maintenance, and more. If you strategy to spend time in your garage this winter tackling projects at your workbench, raising the ambient air temperature is a must.

According to recent reports, garage heaters come in various styles, though the most popular models are electric and propane. Electric heaters are convenient and easy to install if a power outlet is nearby. Propane heaters are more portable and can cover more surface area. Natural gas garage heaters are also powerful options for larger garages and can offer long-term heating solutions.

Industry observers note that heaters can benefit not only comfort but also safety. Cold temps can cause condensation to collect on tools and stored items, which may lead to rust and other damage. Wintry environments can also cause car engines and batteries to wear out faster. A well-heated garage protects your investments and provides a warmer, safer place to work.

If you're ready to prep for winter weather, read on for our in-depth reviews of the best garage heaters, followed by the most important things to know before buying.

Although we haven’t tested the models below ourselves, we applied our experience testing space heaters and patio heaters to supplement our search for the best garage heaters. We spent a lot of time vetting features and specs, checking manufacturer websites, gauging prices, and consulting user reviews before deciding which ones made the cut. We spoke with mechanical and electrical engineering experts to understand what makes a great garage heater, and we considered heat types (electric, propane, or kerosene), as well as whether the heaters are permanent or portable.

This 240-volt compact garage heater is the best all-around choice for most spaces, with 7,500 watts of heating power and the option to mount it on the wall or ceiling.

According to the manufacturer, it warms a typical garage or unheated building to between 50 and 85 degrees Fahrenheit and should be installed with a foot of clearance from combustible surfaces.

Recent findings suggest that the garage heater’s adjustable louvers let you direct air where you need it most, and a remote-controlled thermostat is built into the front of the heater. A wall-mounted thermostat is available for the unit as well, but it’s sold separately.

Thanks to its Wi-Fi capability, you can operate this heater from virtually anywhere to ensure your garage is warm when you get home, or to heat the space before you spend time at your workbench. You can turn the unit on and off and set recurring schedules through the app.

Recent findings suggest that the garage heater is rated to warm a 1,000-square-foot area, with an adjustable output of up to 20,000 BTUs. It can be mounted to the wall or ceiling, and its large digital temperature display is easy to read, even from across the room.

But for the price, it’s disappointing that the garage heater doesn’t include wiring.

Industry observers note that for a powerful 5,600-watt portable garage heater, we recommend this NewAir model. It’s designed to warm spaces up to 600 square feet, and it includes a 6-foot cord that neatly coils on top of the unit, with brackets to hold it down.

The fan has two settings: automatic (which turns on when the heating element activates) and continuous. You can switch between the two manually.

Use continuous mode to keep air moving in spaces with high ceilings or when you’re operating an air-cleaning appliance, like a bench-top air filter, as it helps push dusty air through to speed up the process.

According to recent reports, designed for outdoor areas like patios, this Briza heater still works well in a garage thanks to its dust-resistant properties. It comes with an adjustable tripod that you can set between 44 and 84 inches tall. Selecting between its three heat settings—900, 1,200, or 1,500 watts—is easy with the unit’s remote control.

Recent findings suggest that the heater has a built-in safety sensor that automatically shuts the appliance off if it tips over. A timer provides additional safety (and energy savings) by automatically shutting the heater off after 1 to 9 hours of operation.

It has been revealed that for a compact, affordable garage heater ideal for targeted heating, this propane-fueled unit from Mr. Heater is a great choice. It delivers 4,000 to 9,000 BTUs from a single 1-pound liquid propane canister and can heat up to 250 square feet. It works great on the floor by your workbench or desk.

The heater can run for up to three hours on high, or you can upgrade to a 20-pound tank with a separately sold adapter. The heater’s size and weight make it easy to reposition, and it’s easy to bring with you to a shed, campsite, or other workspace.

This heavy-duty, 240-volt garage heater is ideal for climates with major temperature swings, featuring a two-stage high-and-low heating system.

Its lower heat output suits mildly cool days, while the higher stage can warm garages in single-digit temperatures. It also has a fan mode ideal for increasing airflow in a potentially stuffy garage, plus an energy-saving setting that defaults to the lowest wattage to maintain the desired temperature.

A universal bracket is included for easy mounting to a ceiling or wall, and this heater has a remote-controlled thermostat. The only drawback is that it doesn’t offer much coverage for the price.

If you have an uninsulated wood garage or another minimally insulated space, this large, ceiling-mounted garage heater is worth a look.

It runs on natural gas (a propane conversion kit is included) and, with a built-in electric fan, can warm areas up to 2,000 square feet thanks to its impressive 80,000-BTU output. It also has a powered exhaust that allows for vertical or horizontal venting.

In a recent development, note that the Big Maxx does not come ready to install; you’ll have to purchase a thermostat, gas hose, fittings, and regulator separately. For most people, it’s best to have a licensed heating-cooling contractor install this garage heater.

It has been revealed that there’s a lot to consider when using a heater to keep your garage safe and comfortable. So we picked the brain of Pat Porzio, a mechanical engineer and multi-licensed tradesman (electrical, plumbing, HVAC). He’s also the HVAC manager for Russo Brothers in East Hanover, Upcoming Jersey. We also spoke with David Shapiro, an electrician, author, and expert on old house wiring who contributes to electrical product and installation standards.

Both agree on one thing: Your overarching concern in heating a garage is safety. The first words out of both their mouths were identical: “Pull a permit.” That is, if you plan to use a permanently installed electric or gas-fired garage heater, you need to file a building permit for the work—whether you do the work yourself or hire a contractor. Permitted installations are inspected by the town or other authority with jurisdiction over this work where you live, which increases the likelihood of a safe installation.

Recent findings suggest that aside from pulling a building permit for the electrical work, Shapiro steers homeowners away from any heater without a UL (or other safety-related U.S. testing agency) listing.

In a recent development, using a 120-volt space heater is simpler; same goes for small propane-fired and kerosene heaters. You don’t need a building permit to use one of these in a garage. Still, there are safe and unsafe ways to use these heaters. For more on that topic, check out our garage heater safety tips below.

Sources indicate that as we mentioned earlier, there are a couple of different types of garage heaters. Electric heaters are easier to install, don't require a vent, and are generally safer. But depending on your local electricity rates, they can be more expensive to run. Gas heaters use natural gas or propane, and they can be a more cost-effective option for heating larger garages. They require ventilation, which can be a pain if you don't already have the right setup.

Infrared heaters heat objects rather than the air, so they can be a good companion for localized projects at your workbench. Forced-air heaters use a fan to distribute heat swiftly and work well for large spaces, but they require good insulation to run efficiently and may kick up dust around your workshop.

It has been revealed that for most garages, an electric heater is often the most viable option because it's easy to install, safe, and effective. But if you have a larger or poorly insulated garage, a gas heater might be the way to go.

“A bigger heater is not necessarily better,” Porzio says. “An oversized heater will short cycle. That is, it will turn on and off too frequently. It satisfies heating demand very swiftly and abruptly turns off. A heater that is too small will do just the opposite. It will run and run and never fulfill the heating demand, eventually wearing itself out.”.

Industry observers note that before contractors install a boiler or furnace, they perform a series of calculations, called a Manual J, to determine the correct size. While homeowners can get a rough estimate by multiplying the area's square footage by 50 to get the required BTUs, Porzio recommends using simplified Manual J forms online or a sizing tool like those on King-Electric.com and Newair.com.

For reference, a two-car garage will need a heater ranging from 30,000-50,000 BTUs to reach a consistent, comfortable temperature.

According to recent reports, whether you attempt the electrical work or hire it out, Shapiro has two more recommendations. First, don’t install the heater so that a power cord leading to a machine or tool could be draped directly in front of it. The heat can damage the cord.

Second, consider installing a CO alarm in the garage. A CO alarm can make the garage a safer place to work, especially if you’re heating it with gas, and it can also protect the occupants of the house.

#214724. A fresh discovery could give the world 12 months to prepare for extreme El Niño and La Niña weather events

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1490 w)

A fresh discovery could give the world 12 months to prepare for extreme El Niño and La Niña weather events

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1490 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers have found the conditions needed to predict some El Niño and La Niña events 12 months ahead of time.
  • Most El Niño forecasts are only reliable about six months ahead of time.
  • That is because the Pacific Ocean becomes so sensitive to tiny shifts in the spring that forecast models easily lose track of what comes next.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers have found the conditions needed to predict some El Niño and La Niña events 12 months ahead of time.

Most El Niño forecasts are only reliable about six months ahead of time. Predicting a full year in advance has long been considered nearly impossible.

That is because the Pacific Ocean becomes so sensitive to tiny shifts in the spring that forecast models easily lose track of what comes next.

Now, researchers have found that certain 12-month El Niño forecasts really do hold up, depending on the state of the Pacific on the day the prediction is made.

Forecasts issued during a La Niña held up a year in advance in all nine climate models an Australian team tested. Forecasts issued when the Pacific was in neither phase did worse than a forecast built from nothing but the historical odds.

For farmers and water managers, that could mean months of extra warning before some El Niños.

In a recent development, nandini Ramesh of CSIRO, Australia’s national science agency, and UNSW Sydney led the work. Her co-author Mandy Freund is at the University of Melbourne and the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Weather of the 21st Century.

The team graded about 7,500 past forecasts rather than building a new forecasting system. Ramesh said the researchers are still a few steps from applying the findings to agency models.

Recent findings suggest that in an interview with Earth.com, Freund stated the accuracy of forecasts that started during a La Niña surprised the team most. Routine checks of forecast performance, she said, often don’t sort forecasts by their starting state.

El Niño, La Niña and the neutral years between them make up a cycle scientists call the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or ENSO.

“Separating forecasts according to their starting state, we were able to uncover a much clearer picture of when long-range ENSO predictions can be trusted,” she mentioned.

The warm phase of that cycle is El Niño, when the surface of the central and eastern tropical Pacific runs warmer than usual. La Niña is the cool phase. Both tend to peak around December, and both change weather patterns around the world.

A declared El Niño or La Niña can set off drought warnings for farmers and water managers, the authors wrote. It can move the prices of farm commodities and start public health planning.

By one estimate they cite, seasonal forecasts influence companies worth a combined $13 trillion.

The trouble is the spring. From March to May the tropical Pacific is unusually sensitive to small disturbances. A forecast made before those months and aimed at the winter after them loses much of its skill.

In a recent development, forecasters call this the spring predictability barrier. It is a massive part of why predictions beyond about nine months have stayed so difficult.

The team worked from an archive of decade-long climate simulations run by modeling centers in nine countries. Those include the United States, the United Kingdom, Japan and Canada.

These are physics-based models, which simulate the ocean and atmosphere from physical laws rather than past statistics.

The centers started a fresh batch every year from 1961 to around 2020, and the team used the runs that began between October and January.

Rather than judging the simulations on exact temperatures, the researchers asked one question of each: would the following winter land in La Niña, neutral or El Niño?

They sorted every year into one of those three bins using sea surface temperatures in a patch of the central Pacific. The coolest third of years counted as La Niña and the warmest third as El Niño.

Sorting the years that way left about 7,500 one-year forecasts to grade against NOAA‘s record of what the ocean actually did. Then the researchers split the results by which of the three states the Pacific was in when each forecast began.

In every one of the nine models, forecasts that began during a La Niña scored higher than forecasts that began during an El Niño or a neutral year.

Their skill a year out matched what seasonal forecast models manage three to four months ahead, a range forecasters already rely on.

According to recent reports, forecasts that began from a neutral Pacific did the opposite. In every model, they scored below a forecast built from nothing but the historical odds of one state following another.

Inside a single model, the gap between starting points was larger than the gap between the best and worst models.

“The finding that one-year forecasts starting from La Niña perform well in all nine of the models tested suggests there is something about La Niña conditions that makes the tropical Pacific system more predictable over the following year,” Freund stated.

Stronger La Niña events were predicted better than weaker ones. For El Niño the pattern was less clear, though badly missed forecasts of strong El Niños were rare.

The team then asked the question a farmer might ask of any forecast: when a model predicts a particular switch, how often does it actually happen?

In one American model, a forecast of El Niño issued during a La Niña came true 82 percent of the time, a year ahead of the event. The same model’s forecast of a La Niña from neutral conditions came true only 9 percent of the time.

It has been revealed that three of the nine models were right more than 70 percent of the time when they predicted a La Niña would give way to an El Niño. Eight of the nine were at their worst predicting a La Niña from a neutral year, a switch that is rare in the real ocean.

And when a model called for an El Niño from neutral conditions, not one beat the historical odds. Those calls are the likeliest false alarms.

In a recent development, across all starts from neutral, the models were right 23 to 43 percent of the time. A forecast built from the historical odds alone would have been right 61 percent of the time.

Freund told Earth.com that the weakness from neutral starts remains an important caveat. “Unfortunately, starting from a neutral Pacific, the physics-based models often make the wrong predictions,” she remarked.

“The system can be very sensitive: it is an example of what is known as the ‘butterfly effect’ where very small disturbances can be amplified over time into huge changes in a system’s behavior.”.

Asked by Earth.com what farmers and water managers should take from the result, Freund said the study is encouraging.

In a recent development, those are people, she mentioned, who rely on knowing about an El Niño much further ahead than forecasts now allow. When a La Niña is under way, a forecast for the following year can be trusted more.

“This gives farmers, water managers and other decision-makers valuable extra time to prepare, including decisions about which crops and seed varieties to plant or how to manage water resources,” she said.

Sources indicate that the method itself is simple, Freund said, and would not take much for forecasting agencies to consider. “It could provide this extra layer of confidence we can lay on certain predictions of ENSO,” she said.

The researchers also tested two-year forecasts, and for almost every kind of switch those were wrong more often than right.

The one exception came after an El Niño, when every model did better than the historical odds at saying there would be no El Niño for the next two years. Long stretches without an El Niño have been linked to multi-year droughts across the subtropics.

Why a La Niña makes the following year easier to predict is the open question. The team offered three possibilities.

A La Niña’s cool water tends to linger into spring instead of fading in February or March the way an El Niño’s warmth does. Earlier studies also found fewer random atmospheric disturbances during a La Niña.

And a La Niña is when the upper tropical Pacific refills with warm water, so the state of that reservoir may carry a lot of information about what comes next.

The authors set aside long-term warming trends, slow decade-scale swings in the Pacific and the differences between one El Niño and another.

Sources indicate that they also didn’t test the statistical and machine learning methods they suspect would do better from a neutral start. Those methods work from past patterns instead of from today’s conditions. Whether the La Niña advantage holds in the models agencies actually run each season hasn’t been tested.

Recent findings suggest that the team’s next step is to work out which of the three explanations is doing the work. The confidence check it proposes can be run on any model from the forecasts it has already made.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once remarked.
  • Sources indicate that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer poses in his office on Nov. 9 for a group photo with incoming members of his caucus: from left, Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Texas' James Talarico, Iowa's Josh Turek, Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed, North Carolina's Roy Cooper, Illinois' Juliana Stratton, Latest Hampshire's Chris Pappas, South Carolina's Annie Andrews, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan, Maine's Troy Jackson and Kansas' Adam Hamilton. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

ANALYSIS -- “Life moves pretty fast,” that famed 20th-century philosopher Ferris Bueller once remarked. “If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”.

Sources indicate that in 2024, Democrats were consigned to the political wilderness. Republicans had captured the White House, flipped the Senate and held the House. President Donald Trump had completely altered the party coalitions as he led the ascendant GOP to victory.

Now, just two years later, Democrats are on the rise. A historic midterm tsunami has swept them into such commanding Senate and House majorities that some are questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again. And if Texas is blue, how does the GOP have any chance in the Electoral College again?

A major takeaway from the midterm results should be that there’s very little permanence in our politics.

What may have looked like a newly introduced GOP coalition was really more of a Trump coalition, and it crumbled in the face of economic frustrations, affordability concerns and the president’s unpopular policies.

With Trump’s negative job approval rating weighing them down, Republican candidates suffered losses among virtually all demographic groups – including by wide margins among constituencies thought to make up the GOP’s core.

Trump or the Republicans finished ahead among male voters by 4 points in 2018, 8 points in 2020, 14 points in 2022 and 12 points in 2024, according to the exit polls. Men went for Democratic candidates by 4 points (51 percent to 47 percent) this cycle. Meanwhile, Republicans lost even more ground among women. While Kamala Harris finished ahead of Trump by 8 points in 2024, that margin grew to 21 points for Democratic candidates this year.

Recent findings suggest that trump closed the gap among Hispanic voters to just 5 points behind Harris two years ago. This year, Hispanic voters nationwide supported Democratic candidates by 32 points (65 percent to 33 percent). Even white voters shifted significantly. They backed Trump or  Republican candidates by 10 points in 2018, 17 points in 2020, 18 points in 2022 and 15 points in 2024. And yet Democrats edged out Republicans by a point (50 percent to 49 percent) on Nov. 3.

Voters without a college degree were supposed to be a key cog in Republicans’ newly introduced populist coalition. But they went from +13 (56 percent to 43 percent) for Trump in 2024 to backing Republican candidates by just 1 point this year. Meanwhile, the gap among voters with a college degree went from 14 points for Harris in 2024 to 30 points for Democrats this cycle.

Republicans had closed the gap among young voters aged 18 to 29 from 35 points in 2018 to just 11 points in 2024. But younger voters supported Democratic candidates this year by 50 points (74 percent to 24 percent). Not to mention Democrats flipped voters aged 45 to 64 for the first time in nearly two decades.

White evangelicals appear to be one of the only groups that didn’t shift toward Democrats. They supported GOP candidates 82 percent to 17 percent. But they only made up 17 percent of the electorate, according to the exit polls, which is down from a very consistent 25 percent for more than a decade. So there was still a problem with that group of voters, but it was more about turnout than persuasion.

While there was an unmistakable leftward shift this year, the results should not be considered a permanent party realignment any more than 2024 was. While Democrats did extremely well in Texas this year, they still haven’t won the Lone Star State in a presidential race in 50 years. So maybe it’s wise for everyone to take a deep breath.

In a recent development, if you take this year’s election results and match them with the Senate seats on the ballot in 2028, there doesn’t appear to be a viable path for Republicans back to the majority. But there wasn’t a particularly viable Democratic path to the Senate majority at this point two years ago. And if the Alaska election goes their way, they will end up winning Senate races in seven states that were initially rated Solid Republican.

If one party starts to get too comfortable, voters have a way of bringing politicians back down to earth. If Democrats come to Congress and push too far to the left or become too defined by their most extreme members, they will squander the opportunity they earned this year.

The dramatic demographic swings should be evidence that many voters are not beholden to either party and are open to switching allegiances, particularly in a time of economic uncertainty.

Sources indicate that at the same time, if Republicans don’t go through some time of reflection and instead triple down on the policies that led to the blue wave, they risk cementing some of the shifts that started this cycle. It just won’t be thick cement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 25, 1783, Claude-Louis Mathieu revealed an aptitude for mathematics from a young age.
  • A varied career in astronomy followed, during which Mathieu served as secretary, assistant to the director, and later astronomer at the Paris Observatory, conducting research focused on calculating stars’ parallaxes and determining stellar distances.
  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Born in Macon, France, on Nov. 25, 1783, Claude-Louis Mathieu revealed an aptitude for mathematics from a young age. Despite his family’s poverty and his father’s wish for him to be a carpenter, Mathieu moved to Paris in 1801 to study for admission to the prestigious Ecole Polytechnique. He became a student at Ecole Polytechnique two years later and graduated from the school in 1805.

A varied career in astronomy followed, during which Mathieu served as secretary, assistant to the director, and later astronomer at the Paris Observatory, conducting research focused on calculating stars’ parallaxes and determining stellar distances. He also became a professor of astronomy at the College de France, a writer and editor, and a driving force behind the adoption of the metric system in France. Mathieu was elected president of the International Metre Commission in 1870 although he was in his late 80s, and continued to work in that position into his 90s.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Breaking: A remote island in Latest Zealand was supposed to be a safe haven for wildlife

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth
